claim: Planarians can regenerate their entire CNS using pluripotent adult stem cells.
source: Planarians can regenerate their entire CNS using pluripotent adult stem cells, and this process is robustly regulated to ensure that new neurons are produced in proper abundance.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract describing a known capability of planarians.

claim: tec-1 is a negative regulator of planarian neuronal regeneration.
source: Using a high-throughput pipeline to quantify brain chemosensory neurons, we identify the conserved tyrosine kinase tec-1 as a negative regulator of planarian neuronal regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental screen described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1.

claim: tec-1 RNAi increased the abundance of several CNS and PNS neuron subtypes regenerated or maintained through homeostasis.
source: tec-1RNAi increased the abundance of several CNS and PNS neuron subtypes regenerated or maintained through homeostasis, without affecting body patterning or non-neural cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1 and 3 demonstrating increased neuron numbers after tec-1 RNAi.

claim: tec-1 RNAi does not affect body patterning or non-neural cells.
source: tec-1RNAi increased the abundance of several CNS and PNS neuron subtypes regenerated or maintained through homeostasis, without affecting body patterning or non-neural cells.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 showing no changes in positional control genes and Figure 3—figure supplement 5 showing no changes in muscle or epidermal cells.

claim: tec-1 limits the survival of newly differentiated neurons.
source: Experiments using TUNEL, BrdU, progenitor labeling, and stem cell elimination during regeneration indicate tec-1 limits the survival of newly differentiated neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5, including BrdU labeling, TUNEL staining, and irradiation experiments.

claim: The Tec kinase family has been studied extensively for roles in immune function in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, the Tec kinase family has been studied extensively for roles in immune function, and our results identify a novel role for tec-1 as negative regulator of planarian adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about existing knowledge in the literature regarding Tec kinases.

claim: Adult neural proliferation is absent in C. elegans.
source: Adult neural proliferation is absent in C. elegans and rare in Drosophila, leaving axon repair as a primary mechanism for healing damage to the CNS and PNS.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about C. elegans neural biology.

claim: Adult neural proliferation is rare in Drosophila.
source: Adult neural proliferation is absent in C. elegans and rare in Drosophila, leaving axon repair as a primary mechanism for healing damage to the CNS and PNS.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Drosophila neural biology.

claim: Mammals undergo adult neurogenesis throughout life, but it is limited to particular brain regions and declines with age.
source: Mammals undergo adult neurogenesis throughout life, but it is limited to particular brain regions and declines with age (Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009.

claim: Axolotls and zebrafish are able to repair extensive neural damage.
source: Axolotls and zebrafish are able to repair extensive damage (Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009), while organisms such as planarians and hydra are able to regenerate an entirely new brain through whole-body regeneration (Tanaka and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009.

claim: Planarians and hydra are able to regenerate an entirely new brain through whole-body regeneration.
source: Axolotls and zebrafish are able to repair extensive damage (Tanaka and Ferretti, 2009), while organisms such as planarians and hydra are able to regenerate an entirely new brain through whole-body regeneration (Tanaka and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka and Reddien, 2011.

claim: Whole body regeneration has been proposed to be an ancestral feature based on identification of similar mechanisms of regeneration from the distantly related planarians and acoels.
source: Based on identification of similar mechanisms of regeneration from the distantly related planarians and acoels, whole body regeneration has been proposed to be an ancestral feature (Gehrke and Srivastava, 2016; Reddien, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gehrke and Srivastava, 2016 and Reddien, 2018.

claim: Few negative regulators of neurogenesis have yet been identified.
source: In particular, specific negative regulators of neurogenesis would be important targets for repair enhancement, but few have yet been identified (He and Jin, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to He and Jin, 2016.

claim: Schmidtea mediterranea undergoes complete brain regeneration within 1–2 weeks after injury.
source: The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea undergoes complete brain regeneration within 1–2 weeks after injury and also perpetual homeostatic replacement of brain tissue, making this species an ideal model to identify such factors.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about planarian regeneration.

claim: Schmidtea mediterranea undergoes perpetual homeostatic replacement of brain tissue.
source: The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea undergoes complete brain regeneration within 1–2 weeks after injury and also perpetual homeostatic replacement of brain tissue, making this species an ideal model to identify such factors.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about planarian tissue maintenance.

claim: The planarian brain is composed of an anterior bi-lobed cephalic ganglia with axon-rich neuropils containing interneurons and glia.
source: The planarian brain is composed of an anterior bi-lobed cephalic ganglia with axon-rich neuropils containing interneurons and glia, as well as lateral branches with chemosensory, mechanosensory, and other neurons (Agata et al., 1998; Mineta et al., 2003; Nakazawa et al., 2003; Roberts-Galbraith et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing planarian brain anatomy.

claim: Planarian cell atlas projects recently revealed the existence of ~50 distinct types of neurons.
source: In addition, planarian cell atlas projects recently revealed the existence of ~50 distinct types of neurons, pointing to considerable complexity of regulation for producing and maintaining neurons through ongoing differentiation (Fincher et al., 2018; Plass et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fincher et al., 2018 and Plass et al., 2018.

claim: Planarian tissues are maintained and regenerated by piwi-1+ neoblast stem cells.
source: Planarian tissues are maintained and regenerated by piwi-1+ neoblast stem cells, a mesenchymal cell population found in a parenchymal region and constituting the animal's only proliferative cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about planarian stem cells.

claim: Neoblasts constitute the animal's only proliferative cells.
source: Planarian tissues are maintained and regenerated by piwi-1+ neoblast stem cells, a mesenchymal cell population found in a parenchymal region and constituting the animal's only proliferative cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about planarian cell proliferation.

claim: A subpopulation of TSPN+ neoblasts can give rise to all cell types.
source: Transcriptional profiling and candidate approaches have identified subpopulations of neoblasts specified for participation in distinct tissue lineages including a subpopulation of TSPN+ neoblasts that can give rise to all cell types (Lapan and Reddien, 2011; Cowles et al., 2013; Cowles et al., 2014; Scimone et al., 2014; Brown et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing neoblast subpopulations.

claim: Neural progenitors have been identified as neoblast subpopulations expressing either pro-neurogenic transcription factors or transcription factors expressed in unique differentiated neurons.
source: Neural progenitors have been identified as neoblast subpopulations expressing either pro-neurogenic transcription factors or transcription factors expressed in unique differentiated neurons, and some have been assigned to particular lineages through RNAi (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Molinaro and Pearson, 2016; Fincher et al., 2018; Plass et al., 2018; Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing neural progenitor identification.

claim: Brain regeneration in planarians is a robust process that always ensures a proper restoration of relative neuron abundance in the animal.
source: Brain regeneration in planarians is a robust process that always ensures a proper restoration of relative neuron abundance in the animal.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of planarian regeneration.

claim: Decapitation triggers waves of wound-induced signals, bursts of proliferation, a patterning process to sense missing tissues, and differentiation of new tissues within an outgrowing blastema.
source: Decapitation triggers waves of wound-induced signals, bursts of proliferation, a patterning process to sense missing tissues, and differentiation of new tissues within an outgrowing blastema.
evidence: This is a description of the regeneration process based on established knowledge.

claim: Planarians do not grow appreciably as they regenerate.
source: Planarians do not grow appreciably as they regenerate, so the end of regeneration is characterized by a return to uninjured cell and tissue proportionality with respect to body size (Oviedo et al., 2003; Hill and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oviedo et al., 2003 and Hill and Petersen, 2015.

claim: An RNAi screen of ~50 kinases and receptors with expression enriched in neoblasts was conducted.
source: To identify negative regulators of neuronal regeneration in planarians, we conducted an RNAi screen of ~50 kinases and receptors with expression enriched in neoblasts (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: cto-expressing neurons are arranged in a stereotyped pattern in close proximity to the lateral brain branches.
source: cto-expressing neurons are arranged in a stereotyped pattern in close proximity to the lateral brain branches, and their numbers scale with overall animal and brain size.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of cto+ neurons based on established knowledge.

claim: The numbers of cto-expressing neurons scale with overall animal and brain size.
source: cto-expressing neurons are arranged in a stereotyped pattern in close proximity to the lateral brain branches, and their numbers scale with overall animal and brain size.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of cto+ neurons based on established knowledge.

claim: Treatment with ndk dsRNA produced increased numbers of cto+ cells in the screen.
source: Treatment with a positive control dsRNA targeting ndk, a factor that restricts head regionalization in planarians (Cebrià et al., 2002), produced increased numbers of cto+ cells in the screen.
evidence: This is supported by data from the screen shown in Figure 1B and a citation to Cebrià et al., 2002.

claim: The screen identified four genes whose inhibition reduced numbers of cto+ cells attained through regeneration.
source: The screen identified four genes whose inhibition reduced numbers of cto+ cells attained through regeneration (log2FC < −1 and padj <0.05), though several other treatments caused smaller cto+ cell decreases that did not meet the false-discovery corrected statistical cut-off (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by data from the screen shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Inhibition of tec-1 caused a statistically significant increase in abundance of cto+ cells.
source: We sought to uncover factors that negatively regulated cto+ cell production and found one factor, a Tec-family kinase (tec-1), whose inhibition caused a statistically significant increase in abundance of cto+ cells (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: Inhibition of tec-1 resulted in a robust ~50–100% increase to the number of cto+ cell numbers.
source: These experiments confirmed that inhibition of the Tec homolog resulted in a robust ~50–100% increase to the number of cto+ cell numbers, which had approximately normal spatial distribution in the animal (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: tec-1 knockdown led to an increase in cto+ cell number both in decapitated animals regenerating an entirely new head and also in head fragments undergoing tissue remodeling.
source: tec-1 knockdown led to an increase in cto+ cell number both in decapitated animals regenerating an entirely new head and also in head fragments undergoing tissue remodeling (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increase in relative cto+ cell abundance after tec-1 RNAi was not due to a change in overall animal size, but rather to an increase in absolute numbers of cto+ cells.
source: This increase in relative cto+ cell abundance was not due to a change in overall animal size, but rather to an increase in absolute numbers of cto+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Uninjured planarians undergo perpetual homeostatic regeneration of all cell types, including neurons of the brain, but lack expression of injury induced factors.
source: Uninjured planarians undergo perpetual homeostatic regeneration of all cell types, including neurons of the brain, but lack expression of injury induced factors.
evidence: This is a statement about planarian biology based on established knowledge.

claim: Feeding animals tec-1 dsRNA for 60 days in the absence of injury resulted in cto+ cell number increasing to a similar extent as in amputated fragments.
source: In order to test whether tec-1's function depended on wound signaling, we fed animals tec-1 dsRNA for 60 days in the absence of injury and found that cto+ cell number increased to a similar extent as in amputated fragments (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: tec-1 functions to limit numbers of neurons independent of injury signaling.
source: Therefore, tec-1 functions to limit numbers of neurons independent of injury signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the homeostasis experiment showing increased cto+ cells without injury.

claim: A second Tec family kinase, tec-2, was identified in the Schmidtea mediterranea genome and transcriptome.
source: To examine a possible redundancy of function, we scanned the Schmidtea mediterranea genome and transcriptome and identified a second Tec family kinase, which we named tec-2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inhibition of tec-2 by RNAi did not increase cto+ cell numbers or enhance the effects of tec-1 RNAi.
source: Inhibition of tec-2 by RNAi did not increase cto+ cell numbers or enhance the effects of tec-1 RNAi (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: tec-2 likely does not act redundantly with tec-1 for control of cto+ cell abundance.
source: Therefore, tec-2 likely does not act redundantly with tec-1 for control of cto+ cell abundance.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of tec-2 RNAi on cto+ cell numbers.

claim: RNAi phenotypes that modify body patterning can result in production of excess cto+ cells as a consequence of axis transformation.
source: RNAi phenotypes that modify body patterning (such as nou darake RNAi) can result in production of excess cto+ cells as a consequence of axis transformation (Gurley et al., 2008; Iglesias et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Lander and Petersen, 2016; Scimone et al., 2016), so we tested whether tec-1 could operate similarly.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing patterning effects on cto+ cells.

claim: ndk inhibition increased cto+ cell number concomitant with increasing the size of the brain.
source: Whereas ndk inhibition increased cto+ cell number concomitant with increasing the size of the brain (Cebrià et al., 2002), tec-1 inhibition did not alter brain size (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and a citation to Cebrià et al., 2002.

claim: tec-1 inhibition did not alter brain size.
source: Whereas ndk inhibition increased cto+ cell number concomitant with increasing the size of the brain (Cebrià et al., 2002), tec-1 inhibition did not alter brain size (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: tec-1 RNAi significantly increased the number of cto+ cells normalized to brain size.
source: Instead, tec-1 RNAi, but not ndk RNAi, significantly increased the number of cto+ cells normalized to brain size.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: tec-1 inhibition decreased the average nearest-neighbor distance of cto+ cells.
source: tec-1 inhibition decreased the average nearest-neighbor distance of cto+ cells and also the average volume of each cell as measured by cto mRNA distribution.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: tec-1 inhibition decreased the average volume of cto+ cells as measured by cto mRNA distribution.
source: tec-1 inhibition decreased the average nearest-neighbor distance of cto+ cells and also the average volume of each cell as measured by cto mRNA distribution.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: tec-1 influences cto+ cell abundance and size.
source: Therefore, tec-1 influences cto+ cell abundance and size.
evidence: This is inferred from the measurements of cell density and volume.

claim: tec-1 RNAi did not strongly affect the expression of anterior-posterior positional control genes notum, ndl-3, and wntP-2.
source: To confirm a lack of overall changes to body regionalization in tec-1(RNAi) animals, we examined positional control genes whose expression demarcates distinct body territories. ndl-3 and wntP-2 expression was not appreciably altered in tec-1 RNAi treatments that result in excess cto+ cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: tec-1 inhibition modestly altered the expression of the anteriorly expressed gene notum, which could be attributed to the expansion of a population of notum+chat+ neurons.
source: By WISH, tec-1 inhibition was observed to modestly alter the expression of the anteriorly expressed gene notum, but through FISH analysis this effect could be attributed to the expansion of a population of previously identified notum+chat+ neurons present in the anterior of the brain (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). (Hill and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and a citation to Hill and Petersen, 2015.

claim: tec-1 limits numbers of cto+ cells by altering neuron density rather than participating strongly in body patterning.
source: We conclude that tec-1 limits numbers of cto+ cells by altering neuron density rather than participating strongly in body patterning, and that tec-1 regulates the abundance of more than one type of neuron.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of patterning changes and the increase in neuron density.

claim: tec-1 regulates the abundance of more than one type of neuron.
source: We conclude that tec-1 limits numbers of cto+ cells by altering neuron density rather than participating strongly in body patterning, and that tec-1 regulates the abundance of more than one type of neuron.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased notum+chat+ neurons in addition to cto+ neurons.

claim: glutamic acid decarboxylase (gad) is expressed in GABAergic neurons in the ventral-medial and dorsal-lateral CNS.
source: glutamic acid decarboxylase (gad) is expressed in GABAergic neurons in the ventral-medial and dorsal-lateral CNS (Nishimura et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nishimura et al., 2008b.

claim: Neurons in the ventral-medial and dorsal-lateral CNS domains have distinct progenitor populations expressing nkx2.1 and tcf1 respectively.
source: Neurons in these domains have distinct progenitor populations expressing nkx2.1 and tcf1 respectively (Currie et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Currie et al., 2016 and Brown et al., 2018.

claim: Inhibition of tec-1 increased the total number of GABAergic cells and also numbers of cells within both ventral-medial and dorsal-lateral domains.
source: Inhibition of tec-1 increased the total number of GABAergic cells and also numbers of cells within both domains (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that tec-1's activity is not restricted to a single brain region or a specific neuronal lineage.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: tec-1's activity is not restricted to a single brain region or a specific neuronal lineage.
source: Inhibition of tec-1 increased the total number of GABAergic cells and also numbers of cells within both domains (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that tec-1's activity is not restricted to a single brain region or a specific neuronal lineage.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tec-1 affects multiple neuron populations in different brain regions.

claim: Cephalic ppl-1+ cells increased in abundance after tec-1 knockdown.
source: To confirm this, we quantified cells found throughout the brain which expresses the neuropeptide precursor-encoding gene pyrokinin prohormone-like 1 (ppl-1) (Collins et al., 2010). Cephalic ppl-1+ cells increased in abundance after tec-1 knockdown (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to Collins et al., 2010.

claim: ppl-1 is expressed prominently in neurons of the pharynx, but these cells were unaffected by tec-1 RNAi.
source: ppl-1 is also expressed prominently in neurons of the pharynx, but these cells were unaffected by tec-1 RNAi (Figure 3B), indicating tec-1 does not regulate abundance of all neurons throughout the animal.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: tec-1 does not regulate abundance of all neurons throughout the animal.
source: ppl-1 is also expressed prominently in neurons of the pharynx, but these cells were unaffected by tec-1 RNAi (Figure 3B), indicating tec-1 does not regulate abundance of all neurons throughout the animal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pharyngeal ppl-1+ neurons are not affected by tec-1 RNAi.

claim: The numbers of serotonergic neurons marked by serotonin transporter (sert) increased upon tec-1 inhibition.
source: We additionally examined serotonergic neurons in the CNS marked by serotonin transporter (sert), which have a defined progenitor cell type (Currie and Pearson, 2013; März et al., 2013), and dd17258+ neurons expressed in a domain similar to cto+ cells (Fincher et al., 2018). We observed that the numbers of both of these populations increased upon tec-1 inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citations to Currie and Pearson, 2013; März et al., 2013; and Fincher et al., 2018.

claim: The numbers of dd17258+ neurons increased upon tec-1 inhibition.
source: We additionally examined serotonergic neurons in the CNS marked by serotonin transporter (sert), which have a defined progenitor cell type (Currie and Pearson, 2013; März et al., 2013), and dd17258+ neurons expressed in a domain similar to cto+ cells (Fincher et al., 2018). We observed that the numbers of both of these populations increased upon tec-1 inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to Fincher et al., 2018.

claim: tec-1 RNAi increased the abundance of nociceptory trpA+ neurons in the PNS.
source: To test whether tec-1 might act exclusively within the CNS, we quantified the density of nociceptory trpA+ neurons (Wenemoser et al., 2012; Arenas et al., 2017) and peripheral cholinergic chat+ neurons (Nishimura et al., 2010) of the in the PNS and found that tec-1 RNAi increased the abundance of both cell types (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citations to Wenemoser et al., 2012 and Arenas et al., 2017.

claim: tec-1 RNAi increased the abundance of peripheral cholinergic chat+ neurons in the PNS.
source: To test whether tec-1 might act exclusively within the CNS, we quantified the density of nociceptory trpA+ neurons (Wenemoser et al., 2012; Arenas et al., 2017) and peripheral cholinergic chat+ neurons (Nishimura et al., 2010) of the in the PNS and found that tec-1 RNAi increased the abundance of both cell types (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to Nishimura et al., 2010.

claim: tec-1 knockdown increased the density of dd2223+, dd3733+, and spp-4+ neurons.
source: tec-1 knockdown increased the density of three of these cell types: dd2223+, dd3733+, and spp-4+ neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: tec-1 knockdown did not affect the abundance of dd2723+ neurons, which are expressed in the CNS and pharynx.
source: However, tec-1 knockdown did not affect the abundance of dd2723+ neurons, which are expressed in the CNS and pharynx (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: tec-1(RNAi) animals regenerating a new head sometimes produced disorganized eyes.
source: In addition, we also examined photoreceptor neuron abundance, because tec-1(RNAi) animals regenerating a new head sometimes produced disorganized eyes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: tec-1 inhibition did not modify the number of photoreceptor neurons despite affecting eye morphology.
source: Despite affecting eye morphology, tec-1 inhibition did not modify the number of photoreceptor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: tec-1 inhibition increased the abundance of 10 of 13 neuron markers investigated.
source: Together, we found that tec-1 inhibition increased the abundance of 10 of 13 neuron markers investigated, indicating that tec-1 negatively regulates the abundance of many but not all types of neurons within the central and peripheral nervous systems.
evidence: This is a summary of the data presented in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: tec-1 negatively regulates the abundance of many but not all types of neurons within the central and peripheral nervous systems.
source: Together, we found that tec-1 inhibition increased the abundance of 10 of 13 neuron markers investigated, indicating that tec-1 negatively regulates the abundance of many but not all types of neurons within the central and peripheral nervous systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tec-1 affects multiple but not all neuron types tested.

claim: Planarian proliferative cells have differential sensitivities to DNA damage repair and cell death across the A-P axis.
source: Planarian proliferative cells have differential sensitivities to DNA damage repair and cell death across the A-P axis (Peiris et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peiris et al., 2016.

claim: tec-1 inhibition increased the abundance of dd2223+ neurons in both the anterior and posterior of the animal.
source: To test a potential influence of axis position on the tec-1 RNAi phenotype, we determined the A-P position of all dd2223+ cells in control and tec-1 RNAi animals and binned these into anterior and posterior regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). tec-1 inhibition increased the abundance of dd2223+ neurons in both the anterior and posterior of the animal.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: tec-1 RNAi did not alter the relative proportion of anterior versus posterior dd2223+ neurons.
source: Furthermore, tec-1 RNAi did not alter the relative proportion of anterior versus posterior dd2223+ neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: tec-1 can act equivalently on neurons independent of body position.
source: Together, we conclude that tec-1 can act equivalently on neurons independent of body position.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tec-1 affects neurons equally in anterior and posterior regions.

claim: tec-1 inhibition increased numbers of gad, cto, and ppl-1 neuron cell types to the same extent without affecting gad:cto or ppl1:cto cell ratios.
source: tec-1 inhibition increased numbers of these neuron cell types to the same extent without affecting gad:cto or ppl1:cto cell ratios (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: tec-1 appears to affect multiple neuron type abundances concordantly.
source: Therefore, tec-1 appears to affect multiple neuron type abundances concordantly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ratios between different neuron types remain constant after tec-1 RNAi.

claim: A similar proportion of cto+ cells had processes extending laterally from cell bodies in control versus tec-1(RNAi) animals.
source: A similar proportion of cto+ cells had such processes in control versus tec-1(RNAi) animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: tec-1(RNAi) animals displayed a qualitative increase in size of nerve bundles, particularly evident in the transverse commissural fibers.
source: We also used alpha-tubulin staining to examine overall innervation patterns. In this assay, tec-1(RNAi) animals displayed a qualitative increase in size of nerve bundles, particularly evident in the transverse commissural fibers joining the nerve cords along the ventral side of the animal (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B, 6/7 animals examined).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Treatments disrupting synaptic transmission can cause failure of neuron regeneration in planarians.
source: Treatments disrupting synaptic transmission can cause failure of neuron regeneration in planarians (Inoue et al., 2007), suggesting that the excess neurons in such animals may be functional.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Inoue et al., 2007.

claim: The excess neurons in tec-1(RNAi) animals may be functional.
source: Treatments disrupting synaptic transmission can cause failure of neuron regeneration in planarians (Inoue et al., 2007), suggesting that the excess neurons in such animals may be functional.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that neurons appear morphologically normal and the citation about synaptic transmission.

claim: Neither collagen+ body wall muscle cells nor epidermal nuclei had statistically significant changes in density after tec-1 inhibition.
source: Neither collagen+ body wall muscle cells nor epidermal nuclei were found to have statistically significant changes in density after tec-1 inhibition (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A), suggesting the specificity of tec-1's cell number control activity to the nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The specificity of tec-1's cell number control activity is to the nervous system.
source: Neither collagen+ body wall muscle cells nor epidermal nuclei were found to have statistically significant changes in density after tec-1 inhibition (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A), suggesting the specificity of tec-1's cell number control activity to the nervous system.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect on non-neural cell types.

claim: There were not obvious increases in expression of markers of excretory and intestinal tissue after tec-1 inhibition.
source: We also examined animals stained for broad markers of excretory and intestinal tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B). There were not obvious increases in expression of either marker of these tissue types.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claim: tec-1 inhibition decreased the density of cells expressing pooled glial markers intermediate filament 1 (if-1) and calamari (cali).
source: In addition, we also examined non-neuronal cells in the CNS characterized as astrocyte-like glial cells (Roberts-Galbraith et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016). tec-1 inhibition decreased the density of cells expressing pooled glial markers intermediate filament 1 (if-1) and calamari (cali) as well as those expressing glucose transporter (glut) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and citations to Roberts-Galbraith et al., 2016 and Wang et al., 2016.

claim: tec-1 inhibition decreased the density of cells expressing glucose transporter (glut).
source: In addition, we also examined non-neuronal cells in the CNS characterized as astrocyte-like glial cells (Roberts-Galbraith et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016). tec-1 inhibition decreased the density of cells expressing pooled glial markers intermediate filament 1 (if-1) and calamari (cali) as well as those expressing glucose transporter (glut) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and citations to Roberts-Galbraith et al., 2016 and Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Planarian glial cells could have a role in neuron surveillance.
source: The functions for planarian glial cells are not yet characterized, but these cells could have a role in neuron surveillance.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential function of glial cells.

claim: Differentiated cells are produced continually from neoblasts in adult planarians.
source: Differentiated cells are produced continually from neoblasts in adult planarians, so that increases to numbers of differentiated cells could either arise from an increase in stem cell-dependent tissue production or through decreases in the death of differentiated cells.
evidence: This is a statement about planarian biology based on established knowledge.

claim: Neurons and glial cells can arise from common progenitor cells in some contexts in other organisms.
source: Because tec-1 knockdown broadly increased neuronal numbers while decreasing glial numbers, and it is known that neurons and glial cells can arise from common progenitor cells in some contexts in other organisms, we initially hypothesized that tec-1 might control a differentiation switch at some early point in neural specification (Mori et al., 2005; Homem and Knoblich, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mori et al., 2005 and Homem and Knoblich, 2012.

claim: In decapitated tec-1(RNAi) animals regenerating a new head, the rate of production of new cto+ cells was not altered at early times (4 days).
source: In decapitated tec-1(RNAi) animals regenerating a new head, the rate of production of new cto+ cells was not altered at early times (4 days), but abundance of cto+ cells was higher after a week of regeneration (8 days) and reached a maximum point at 16 days.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In decapitated tec-1(RNAi) animals regenerating a new head, abundance of cto+ cells was higher after a week of regeneration (8 days) and reached a maximum point at 16 days.
source: In decapitated tec-1(RNAi) animals regenerating a new head, the rate of production of new cto+ cells was not altered at early times (4 days), but abundance of cto+ cells was higher after a week of regeneration (8 days) and reached a maximum point at 16 days.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: tec-1 is expressed broadly in the animal and throughout regeneration from day 2 to day 12 post-amputation without undergoing discernable regeneration-induced expression changes.
source: We also confirmed through WISH that tec-1 is expressed broadly in the animal and throughout regeneration from day 2 to day 12 post-amputation without undergoing discernable regeneration-induced expression changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: tec-1 likely functions constitutively to regulate neuron numbers.
source: Given this expression and that tec-1 affects neuron density in both regeneration and homeostasis, it is likely this gene functions constitutively to regulate neuron numbers.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern and functional data.

claim: cto cells had reached a steady-state maximum by two weeks post-amputation.
source: To test for the perdurance of the phenotype in regeneration, we measured cto+ cell number up to 4 weeks after decapitation and found that cto cells had reached a steady-state maximum by two weeks post-amputation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In tec-1(RNAi) head fragments undergoing tissue remodeling, the maximal cto+ cell abundance phenotype was observed by 4 days and persisted.
source: In tec-1(RNAi) head fragments undergoing tissue remodeling, the maximal cto+ cell abundance phenotype was observed somewhat earlier, by 4 days, and persisted (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The progressive nature of the phenotype in decapitated regenerating animals suggests that tec-1 is unlikely to regulate rates of differentiation commonly across all timescales and conditions.
source: The progressive nature of the phenotype in decapitated regenerating animals suggests that tec-1 is unlikely to regulate rates of differentiation commonly across all timescales and conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the time course data showing delayed phenotype onset.

claim: Neoblasts are the only proliferative cells in adult planarians.
source: Neoblasts are the only proliferative cells in adult planarians, so a pulse of BrdU initially marks these cells, followed by labeling their newly-born post-mitotic descendants (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2000).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation to Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2000.

claim: Numbers of ppl-1+BrdU+ cells were not significantly different in control versus tec-1(RNAi) animals over a range of timepoints of BrdU pulsing and fixation in regeneration.
source: However, numbers of ppl-1+BrdU+ cells were not significantly different in control versus tec-1(RNAi) animals over a range of timepoints of BrdU pulsing and fixation in regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: tec-1 inhibition can increase numbers of neurons without modifying rates of differentiation, pointing instead to a function in controlling neuron survival.
source: These data indicate that tec-1 inhibition can increase numbers of neurons without modifying rates of differentiation, pointing instead to a function in controlling neuron survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the BrdU labeling data showing no change in differentiation rates.

claim: A model in which tec-1 controls neuronal survival would predict that tec-1 does not influence the abundance of neural progenitor cells.
source: A model in which tec-1 controls neuronal survival would predict that tec-1 does not influence the abundance of neural progenitor cells that are the intermediates between pluripotent neoblast stem cells and differentiated neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: coe encodes a transcription factor expressed in a subpopulation of piwi-1+ neoblasts as well as in a variety of differentiated neurons.
source: coe encodes a transcription factor expressed in a subpopulation of piwi-1+ neoblasts as well as in a variety of differentiated neurons, and its inhibition reduces the abundance of several types of neurons, including gad+ and cto+ neurons (Cowles et al., 2013; Cowles et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cowles et al., 2013 and Cowles et al., 2014.

claim: tec-1 inhibition did not alter numbers of coe+piwi-1+ cells in a timeseries between 2 and 12 days of head regeneration.
source: tec-1 inhibition did not alter numbers of coe+piwi-1+ cells in a timeseries between 2 and 12 days of head regeneration, despite detection of an overall decreasing abundance of such progenitors in both control and tec-1(RNAi) animals over time as regeneration proceeds.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The abundance of pax6+piwi-1+ neoblasts was unaltered by tec-1 inhibition.
source: To confirm these observations, we examined a subpopulation of piwi-1+ neoblasts expressing the proneural transcription factor pax6 (Scimone et al., 2014) and found that its abundance was also unaltered by tec-1 inhibition in the same time period.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to Scimone et al., 2014.

claim: pitx transcription factor is required for production of sert+ serotonergic neurons.
source: pitx transcription factor is required for production of sert+ serotonergic neurons and pitx is expressed within a piwi-1+ neoblast subpopulation proposed to be the progenitors for these cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of pitx based on established knowledge.

claim: tec-1 RNAi did not alter numbers of pitx+piwi-1+ serotonergic neuron progenitors near the brain.
source: Although tec-1 inhibition increased the abundance of sert+ neurons in the brain (Figure 3A), tec-1 RNAi did not alter numbers of pitx+piwi-1+ serotonergic neuron progenitors near the brain (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: tec-1 FISH signal was detected within each type of neuron tested (cto, gad, ppl-1), within pitx, coe, or pax6A-expressing cells, neoblasts or their differentiating progeny marked with anti-PIWI-1 antibody, and in if-1;cali+ glial cells.
source: However, we detected tec-1 FISH signal not only within each type of neuron tested (cto, gad, ppl-1) but also within pitx, coe, or pax6A-expressing cells, neoblasts or their differentiating progeny marked with anti-PIWI-1 antibody, and in if-1;cali+ glial cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: tec-1 is a broadly expressed gene that exerts a specific effect on neuronal cell density.
source: Therefore, tec-1 is a broadly expressed gene that exerts a specific effect on neuronal cell density.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern and functional specificity.

claim: tec-1 inhibition did not modify numbers of H3P+ mitotically active cells in response to injury.
source: Consistent with these observations and the specificity of the tec-1(RNAi) phenotype, tec-1 inhibition did not modify numbers of H3P+ mitotically active cells in response to injury (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: These results support the model that tec-1 does not regulate the process of neuronal differentiation or control a switch between neuronal and glial specification.
source: Taken together, these results support the model that tec-1 does not regulate the process of neuronal differentiation or control a switch between neuronal and glial specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effects on progenitor numbers and differentiation rates.

claim: Uninjured planarians undergo a basal rate of homeostatic cell death thought to occur across tissue types as older cells die off and require stem cell-dependent replacement.
source: Uninjured planarians undergo a basal rate of homeostatic cell death thought to occur across tissue types as older cells die off and require stem cell-dependent replacement, and amputation triggers a systemic elevation of cell death of differentiated cells as part of the tissue remodeling process (Pellettieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: Amputation triggers a systemic elevation of cell death of differentiated cells as part of the tissue remodeling process.
source: Uninjured planarians undergo a basal rate of homeostatic cell death thought to occur across tissue types as older cells die off and require stem cell-dependent replacement, and amputation triggers a systemic elevation of cell death of differentiated cells as part of the tissue remodeling process (Pellettieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: tec-1 RNAi reduced but did not eliminate numbers of TUNEL+ cells.
source: We used TUNEL staining on remodeling head fragments to test whether tec-1 promotes cell death and found that tec-1 RNAi reduced but did not eliminate numbers of TUNEL+ cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The observation that tec-1 RNAi reduces TUNEL+ cells is consistent with a model in which tec-1 promotes cell death of some but not all cells.
source: This observation is consistent with a model in which tec-1 promotes cell death of some but not all cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the TUNEL data showing partial reduction in cell death.

claim: In control animals, the density of cto+ neurons decreased between four and six days after irradiation.
source: In control animals, the density of cto+ neurons (red) decreased between four and six days after irradiation (bracket).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: tec-1(RNAi) animals had normal numbers of newly formed cintillo+ cells at d10 post amputation, but significantly greater numbers than controls two days later.
source: By contrast, tec-1(RNAi) animals had normal numbers of newly formed cintillo+ cells, cto+ number is not significantly greater than controls at d10 post amputation, but is significantly greater than controls two days later.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: These data confirm that tec-1 does not influence rates of cell production but instead strongly suggest that tec-1 promotes the death of newly born neurons in order to limit the abundance of cells produced through adult neurogenesis.
source: These data confirm that tec-1 does not influence rates of cell production but instead strongly suggest that tec-1 promotes the death of newly born neurons in order to limit the abundance of cells produced through adult neurogenesis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from the irradiation experiment showing differential survival of neurons.

claim: Completion of regeneration and homeostatic maintenance requires control of both the rates of new cell differentiation and also control of cell survival.
source: Completion of regeneration and homeostatic maintenance requires control of both the rates of new cell differentiation and also control of cell survival (LoCascio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to LoCascio et al., 2017.

claim: Injuries trigger expression of the runt-1 transcription factor within neoblasts, required for producing normal numbers of trpA+ brain cells, eyes, and other cells.
source: Injuries trigger expression of the runt-1 transcription factor within neoblasts, required for producing normal numbers of trpA+ brain cells, eyes, and other cells.
evidence: This is a statement about runt-1 function based on established knowledge.

claim: Inhibition of bcl2-1, a conserved antiapoptotic factor, causes a rapid increase in systemic cell death and subsequent animal lysis.
source: Inhibition of bcl2-1, a conserved antiapoptotic factor, causes a rapid increase in systemic cell death and subsequent animal lysis (Pellettieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pellettieri et al., 2010.

claim: jnk and yorkie inhibition both decrease cell death and increase numbers of cto+ cells relative to overall body size in decapitated head fragments.
source: jnk and yorkie inhibition both decrease cell death and increase numbers of cto+ cells relative to overall body size in decapitated head fragments (Almuedo-Castillo et al., 2014; Lin and Pearson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Almuedo-Castillo et al., 2014 and Lin and Pearson, 2014.

claim: In jnk and yorkie inhibition phenotypes, an increase in neuronal number is linked to an increase in overall brain size and is in a context in which the brain normally undergoes reduction through injury-induced remodeling.
source: However, in both of these phenotypes, an increase in neuronal number is linked to an increase in overall brain size and is in a context in which the brain normally undergoes reduction through injury-induced remodeling.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of jnk and yorkie phenotypes.

claim: Based on tec-1's specificity for neural cells and utilization in both regeneration and homeostasis, it operates in a distinct pathway from jnk and yorkie.
source: Based on tec-1's specificity for neural cells and utilization in both regeneration and homeostasis, we suggest it operates in a distinct pathway (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from the differences between tec-1 and jnk/yorkie phenotypes.

claim: The broad expression of tec-1 throughout multiple tissues would be consistent with either cell autonomous action within neurons or action within a distinct cell population involved in neuron killing and/or engulfment.
source: The broad expression of tec-1 throughout multiple tissues would be consistent with either possibility (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms based on expression data.

claim: Cell atlas projects found that tec-1 is expressed broadly but is moderately enriched in neural progenitors.
source: Cell atlas projects also found that tec-1 is expressed broadly but is moderately enriched in neural progenitors, consistent with the first possibility, but also within intestine and cathepsin+ cells that could have uncharacterized roles in neuron homeostasis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) (Fincher et al., 2018; Plass et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and citations to Fincher et al., 2018 and Plass et al., 2018.

claim: Tec family kinases (TFKs) are non-receptor tyrosine kinases similar to Src family kinases.
source: Tec family kinases (TFKs) are non-receptor tyrosine kinases similar to Src family kinases.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about TFKs.

claim: TFKs are perhaps best known for signaling downstream of antigen receptors in hematopoietic differentiation and lymphomas.
source: TFKs are perhaps best known for signaling downstream of antigen receptors in hematopoietic differentiation and lymphomas (Berg et al., 2005; Rickert, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berg et al., 2005 and Rickert, 2013.

claim: Tec kinases are involved in a wide variety of signaling pathways downstream of GPCRs, integrins, and both receptor and non-receptor tyrosine kinases.
source: However, they are also involved in a wide variety of signaling pathways downstream of GPCRs, integrins, and both receptor and non-receptor tyrosine kinases, and are known to regulate apoptosis, cell adhesion, and the actin cytoskeleton in addition to differentiation (Takesono et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Takesono et al., 2002.

claim: In mammals, a majority of studies have found that Tec kinases such as BTK are essential for the survival or proliferation of immune cells, including phagocytic cells.
source: In mammals, a majority of studies have found that Tec kinases such as BTK are essential for the survival or proliferation of immune cells, including phagocytic cells (Takesono et al., 2004; Jongstra-Bilen et al., 2008; Melcher et al., 2008; Palmer et al., 2008), suggesting that planarian tec-1 might not act cell autonomously within neurons to promote death.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing Tec kinase functions in immune cells.

claim: In some contexts, Tec kinases have been reported to function as cell autonomous tumor suppressor genes that promote p53-mediated cell death pathways.
source: Alternatively, in some contexts, Tec kinases have been reported to function as cell autonomous tumor suppressor genes that promote p53-mediated cell death pathways (Rada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rada et al., 2018.

claim: Chemical inhibition of the Tec-family kinase BTK increased brain cell survival after ischemic brain injury, an effect attributed to the modification of macrophage activity.
source: Within the mammalian brain, chemical inhibition of the Tec-family kinase BTK increased brain cell survival after ischemic brain injury, an effect attributed to the modification of macrophage activity (Ito et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ito et al., 2015.

claim: It is possible that Tec kinases could regulate conserved functions in adult neurogenesis to control of neuron abundance in other organisms.
source: It is possible that Tec kinases could regulate conserved functions in adult neurogenesis to control of neuron abundance in other organisms.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential conservation of tec-1 function.

claim: The requirement for tec-1 for neuron suppression in regeneration and homeostasis in planarians suggests that developmental cell death of neurons might be a common feature of adult neurogenesis across species.
source: The requirement for tec-1 for neuron suppression in regeneration and homeostasis in planarians additionally suggests that developmental cell death of neurons might be a common feature of adult neurogenesis across species.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in planarians.

claim: Cell death is extensively used throughout the animal kingdom to sculpt the developing nervous system, from nematodes to mammals.
source: Cell death is extensively used throughout the animal kingdom to sculpt the developing nervous system, from nematodes to mammals (Yamaguchi and Miura, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yamaguchi and Miura, 2015.

claim: Adult neurogenesis has been detected in Drosophila within the medulla cortex, where it can also mediate injury repair.
source: Among well-studied invertebrates, adult neurogenesis has been detected in Drosophila within the medulla cortex, where it can also mediate injury repair (Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fernández-Hernández et al., 2013.

claim: The bulk of neurogenesis in C. elegans and Drosophila occurs at embryonic or larval stages prior to adulthood.
source: However, the bulk of neurogenesis in C. elegans and Drosophila occurs at embryonic or larval stages prior to adulthood, so the precise roles of cell death for adult neurogenesis and ways they may be conserved across distant phyla have yet to be fully elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about neurogenesis timing in these organisms.

claim: Based on TUNEL staining and mouse mutants defective for cell death in the nervous system, developmental cell death of neurons is integral to adult neurogenesis in mammals.
source: Based on TUNEL staining and the observation that mouse mutants defective for cell death in the nervous system overproduce neurons in multiple regions of the brain, developmental cell death of neurons is integral to adult neurogenesis in mammals (Biebl et al., 2000; Winner et al., 2002; Sun et al., 2004), and cell death after differentiation has been confirmed through direct observation (Pilz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing cell death in mammalian neurogenesis.

claim: Regulation of cell death at the level of neural progenitors may control brain morphology by preventing hyperplasia or may define where crucial morphogenic signals are expressed.
source: Regulation of cell death at the level of neural progenitors may control brain morphology by preventing hyperplasia or may define where crucial morphogenic signals are expressed (Haydar et al., 1999; Nonomura et al., 2013; Yamaguchi and Miura, 2015), while regulation of the survival of newly formed neurons has been proposed to provide mechanisms to ensure proper connectivity or limit interneuron cell number (Southwell et al., 2012; Dekkers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing roles of cell death in neural development.

claim: Regulation of the survival of newly formed neurons has been proposed to provide mechanisms to ensure proper connectivity or limit interneuron cell number.
source: Regulation of cell death at the level of neural progenitors may control brain morphology by preventing hyperplasia or may define where crucial morphogenic signals are expressed (Haydar et al., 1999; Nonomura et al., 2013; Yamaguchi and Miura, 2015), while regulation of the survival of newly formed neurons has been proposed to provide mechanisms to ensure proper connectivity or limit interneuron cell number (Southwell et al., 2012; Dekkers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Southwell et al., 2012 and Dekkers et al., 2013.

claim: During brain development, preventing neurotransmitter secretion results in assembly of a mostly normal brain followed by massive neuronal apoptosis.
source: During brain development, preventing neurotransmitter secretion results in assembly of a mostly normal brain followed by massive neuronal apoptosis, suggesting that regulated cell death plays a role in the maturation of newly-differentiated neurons during embryogenesis (Verhage et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Verhage et al., 2000.

claim: Reliance on neurotransmitter signaling to promote survival of immature neurons is also used extensively in murine adult neurogenesis.
source: Reliance on neurotransmitter signaling to promote survival of immature neurons is also used extensively in murine adult neurogenesis (Petreanu and Alvarez-Buylla, 2002), among other cell-type specific mechanisms (Pfisterer and Khodosevich, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Petreanu and Alvarez-Buylla, 2002 and Pfisterer and Khodosevich, 2017.

claim: Many cell survival pathways converge on promoting survival through BCL2 family members, while death is promoted by Bax and Bak.
source: Many of these pathways converge on promoting survival through BCL2 family members, while death is promoted by Bax and Bak (Motoyama et al., 1995; Shindler et al., 1997; Sun et al., 2004; Savitt et al., 2005; Nakamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing cell death pathways.

claim: Inhibitors of core cell death pathways have been proposed as therapeutic agents to assist in damage repair after brain injury.
source: Therefore, inhibitors of core cell death pathways have been proposed as therapeutic agents to assist in damage repair after brain injury (Degterev et al., 2005; Loane and Faden, 2010), though these would be expected to have substantial effects on other organ systems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degterev et al., 2005 and Loane and Faden, 2010.

claim: If the ability of Tec kinases to limit neuron production ultimately proves to be conserved, they would be potential targets for enhancing neural repair in other species.
source: If the ability of Tec kinases to limit neuron production ultimately proves to be conserved, they would be potential targets for enhancing neural repair in other species.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential therapeutic application of the findings.

claim: Suppressors of mTOR and JAK/STAT signaling in vertebrates can be inhibited to increase axon growth after spinal cord injury in laboratory conditions.
source: Suppressors of mTOR and JAK/STAT signaling in vertebrates can be inhibited to increase axon growth after spinal cord injury in laboratory conditions (Park et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Park et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2010; and Sun et al., 2011.

claim: The JAK/STAT inhibitors Socs3 and Sfpq attenuate axonal regrowth in the optic nerve of mice and zebrafish.
source: The JAK/STAT inhibitors Socs3 and Sfpq attenuate axonal regrowth in the optic nerve of mice and zebrafish (Smith et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2011; Elsaeidi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2011; and Elsaeidi et al., 2014.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling appears to promote neural regeneration in vertebrates.
source: Additionally, while canonical Wnt signaling appears to promote neural regeneration in vertebrates (Yin et al., 2008; Strand et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2017), non-canonical Wnt signaling inhibits axon guidance and growth (Onishi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yin et al., 2008; Strand et al., 2016; and Patel et al., 2017.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt signaling inhibits axon guidance and growth.
source: Additionally, while canonical Wnt signaling appears to promote neural regeneration in vertebrates (Yin et al., 2008; Strand et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2017), non-canonical Wnt signaling inhibits axon guidance and growth (Onishi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Onishi et al., 2014.

claim: A more complete understanding of negative inputs into adult tissue homeostasis could provide new and more specific targets for the enhancement of neural tissue repair or treatment of degenerative disease.
source: A more complete understanding of negative inputs into adult tissue homeostasis could provide new and more specific targets for the enhancement of neural tissue repair or treatment of degenerative disease (Trounson and McDonald, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Trounson and McDonald, 2015.

claim: Planarians, which undergo extensive homeostasis of the CNS in adulthood, can be a model for efficiently identifying negative regulators of adult neurogenesis.
source: Our results suggest that planarians, which undergo extensive homeostasis of the CNS in adulthood, can be a model for efficiently identifying such negative regulators of adult neurogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful identification of tec-1 as a negative regulator.
